data.title: Correct ModelArray stacking semantics
data.body:
## Goal
- Make stacking create a leading axis while preserving every source array shape and model.
- Keep concatenation behavior explicit instead of hiding it behind stack terminology.

## Acceptance Criteria
- StackModelArrays requires equal non-empty shapes and returns [count]+shape.
- Model ordering and metadata copying are preserved.
- Shape mismatch, nil arrays, and empty input have deterministic errors.
- README examples and behavioral tests describe true stacking.

## Validation Gates
- go test -run 'ModelArray|Stack'
- go vet ./...

data.title: Make passivity results mathematically honest
data.body:
## Goal
- Distinguish finite-grid passivity evidence from analytic certification.
- Preserve compatibility while preventing sampled checks from presenting themselves as proofs.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Results disclose whether they are sampled or certified and retain the checked frequency range/grid.
- State-space and FRD checks use correct Hermitian-part eigenvalue criteria for MIMO systems.
- Tests cover narrow-band or out-of-range counterexamples and invalid grids.
- Documentation states the exact guarantee.

## Validation Gates
- go test -run 'Passiv|Spectral'
- go vet ./...

data.title: Implement basis-invariant modal truncation
data.body:
## Goal
- Replace state-index deletion with a real ordered modal/Schur reduction workflow.
- Preserve complex-conjugate blocks and descriptor-system correctness or reject unsupported cases explicitly.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Mode selection controls retained modal blocks rather than source coordinates.
- Similarity-equivalent realizations retain the same selected poles and equivalent reduced responses.
- Complex conjugate pairs are never split; unstable-mode policy is explicit.
- Tests use coupled non-symmetric systems and compare pole/response invariants.

## Validation Gates
- go test -run 'Modal|Modred'
- go test -race -run 'Modal|Modred'
- go vet ./...

data.title: Assemble physical port connections into dynamics
data.body:
## Goal
- Make physical connections and grounding alter the assembled equations rather than only validate metadata.
- Give assembly one owner for topology, constraints, elimination, and external-port construction.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Connected and disconnected component assemblies have demonstrably different transfer behavior.
- Compatible through/across port equations and grounding are represented mathematically.
- Invalid, duplicate, underdetermined, and overconstrained topologies return actionable errors.
- Descriptor constraints are preserved when algebraic elimination is not valid.
- Tests cover coupling, grounding, multi-component topology, and non-symmetric dynamics.

## Validation Gates
- go test -run 'Physical|Assembly|Port'
- go test -race -run 'Physical|Assembly|Port'
- go vet ./...

data.title: Replace inverse-based DARE with a generalized Schur solve
data.body:
## Goal
Make the discrete algebraic Riccati solver robust when A is singular or ill-conditioned by owning the full generalized symplectic-pencil workflow inside the Riccati module.

## Context
The current DARE path explicitly forms inverse-transpose(A), which rejects solvable singular-A problems and amplifies conditioning errors. SLICOT SB02OD uses an ordered generalized-Schur/deflating-subspace method, and the pinned Gonum fork provides the required Dgges/Dtgsen-class machinery.

## Acceptance criteria
- The implementation no longer computes an explicit inverse of A.
- Persistent tests cover singular-A and ill-conditioned, non-symmetric DARE cases with fixed values produced by an independent oracle.
- The returned X is symmetric, the scaled Riccati residual meets the existing tolerance policy, and the closed-loop eigenvalues are strictly inside the unit circle for stabilizing cases.
- Existing CARE/DARE APIs, workspace reuse, error semantics, and allocation expectations remain compatible.
- Focused benchmarks show no material regression on existing representative DARE sizes.

## Validation gates
- Run focused Riccati tests and oracle fixtures.
- Run focused before/after DARE benchmarks through benchstat.
- Run go fix ./..., go vet ./..., and go test -v -count=1.

data.title: Deepen the frequency-sweep evaluator
data.body:
## Goal
Make frequencyEvaluator own backend selection and reusable sweep workspaces so repeated frequencies do not rebuild transfer-function realizations unnecessarily.

## Context
Profiles show newTFWorkspace dominates allocation in FreqResponse and tuning. The evaluator currently converts a state-space model to transfer functions for multi-point sweeps, while single-point evaluation uses a reusable state-space solve. The LFT kernel also performs one duplicate diagonal multiply.

## Acceptance criteria
- frequencyEvaluator selects an evidence-backed state-space or transfer-function kernel based on model/grid shape, with the decision hidden from callers.
- Sweep workspaces are allocated once per response operation and reused across frequencies.
- The duplicate LFT diagonal multiply is removed.
- Persistent parity tests cover both selected kernels, non-symmetric A, continuous/discrete models, descriptor models, delays, and LFT responses.
- Numerical error is no worse than the current implementation against the existing reference behavior.
- Focused FreqResponse and LFT benchmarks show lower allocations and no material time regression across representative small and larger systems.

## Validation gates
- Run focused frequency tests.
- Run focused before/after frequency and LFT benchmarks through benchstat.
- Run go fix ./..., go vet ./..., and go test -v -count=1.

data.title: Make physical assembly own matrices once
data.body:

Move physical-model copy and validation ownership into physicalAssemblyPlan so assembly crosses one ownership boundary instead of cloning components and aggregate matrices repeatedly.

The current path copies every component, copies into aggregate matrices, then the Descriptor constructor copies the aggregate again. The synchronous assembly plan can validate inputs while building an owned aggregate result directly.

## Validation gates

data.title: Add generalized-Schur DARE for singular and ill-conditioned models

data.body:
## Goal
Make the discrete algebraic Riccati solver robust when A is singular or ill-conditioned while preserving the fast path for well-conditioned models.

## Context
The former DARE path rejected solvable singular-A problems. An always-generalized implementation fixed that but caused a material pure-Go QZ allocation and runtime regression. The Riccati module now owns a condition-based kernel choice: the existing symplectic Schur reduction for well-conditioned A and a SLICOT/SciPy-style extended symplectic pencil for singular or poorly conditioned A.

## Acceptance criteria
- Singular and poorly conditioned A use an ordered generalized-Schur deflating-subspace solve.
- Well-conditioned models retain the established fast Schur kernel behind the same private owner.
- Persistent tests cover singular-A cross-term and ill-conditioned, non-symmetric DARE cases with fixed values produced by an independent SciPy oracle.
- The returned X is symmetric, the scaled Riccati residual meets the existing tolerance policy, and the closed-loop eigenvalues are strictly inside the unit circle for stabilizing cases.
- Existing CARE/DARE APIs, workspace reuse, and error semantics remain compatible.
- Focused benchmarks show no material regression on existing representative DARE sizes.

## Validation gates
- Run focused Riccati tests and oracle fixtures.
- Run focused before/after DARE benchmarks through benchstat.
- Run go fix ./..., go vet ./..., and go test -v -count=1.

## Completion note
- Added a private discrete-stable-subspace owner that chooses the regular or generalized kernel from the reciprocal condition estimate of A.
- Implemented the extended symplectic pencil, QR input-column deflation, ordered generalized Schur solve, and generalized eigenvalue recovery.
- Added singular cross-term and ill-conditioned non-symmetric SciPy oracle fixtures and corrected the cross-term residual helper.
- Ten-sample benchstat: n=10 timing unchanged; n=50 +2.37%; allocation counts unchanged and bytes decreased slightly.

## Goal
Make frequencyEvaluator own backend selection and reusable sweep workspaces so short sweeps avoid rebuilding transfer-function realizations while long sweeps keep polynomial-evaluation throughput.

## Context
Profiles showed newTFWorkspace dominated FreqResponse allocation, but always using direct state-space solves materially slowed longer grids. Persistent kernel benchmarks established a crossover governed primarily by state count times frequency count. The evaluator now owns that choice and falls back to transfer-function evaluation if a direct sweep encounters a pole.

## Acceptance criteria
- frequencyEvaluator selects the state-space or transfer-function kernel from an evidence-backed work limit hidden from callers.
- State-space sweep workspaces are allocated once per response operation and reused across frequencies.
- Persistent parity tests cover both selected kernels, a non-symmetric A, delay phases, descriptor evaluation, continuous/discrete behavior, and pole fallback.
- Numerical error is no worse than EvalFr within the established tolerance.
- Focused FreqResponse benchmarks show lower allocations and runtime for short sweeps with no material regression for longer, delayed, or LFT sweeps.

## Validation gates
- Run focused frequency tests.
- Run focused before/after frequency and LFT benchmarks through benchstat.
- Run go fix ./..., go vet ./..., and go test -v -count=1.

## Completion note
- Added private state-space and transfer-function sweep kernels under frequencyEvaluator and a conservative state-count by frequency-count work policy.
- Added transfer-function fallback when a short direct sweep reaches a pole, preserving multi-frequency behavior.
- Added persistent kernel-crossover and public short-sweep benchmarks plus parity coverage for both kernels and all delay forms.
- Ten-sample benchstat for the 10-state, 8-frequency case: runtime -42.19%, bytes -85.74%, allocations -94.44%. Long, delayed, B747, and LFT sweeps were unchanged within noise.
- The duplicate LFT multiply noted during initial planning was already absent after synchronizing with origin/main, so no LFT code change was needed.

# Unify complex singular-value evaluation

## Goal
Give the frequency-analysis numerical module one reusable singular-value implementation and make tuning goals consume flat response storage without per-frequency matrix cloning.

## Context
tuning_goal.go duplicated complex singular-value logic using mat.SVD and Values(nil), while frequency_svd.go already owned reusable buffers for Sigma and FRD operations. The duplicate path allocated heavily and could drift numerically.

## Acceptance criteria
- One internal complex-SVD workspace owns singular-value evaluation for Sigma, FRD, and tuning goals.
- Tuning consumes stride-correct flat frequency-response slices without constructing a new matrix per frequency.
- Persistent tests compare maximum singular values against Gonum SVD over rectangular, rank-deficient, scaled, and non-symmetric complex matrices.
- Existing tuning-goal values and tolerances are preserved or improved.
- Focused tuning benchmarks show lower allocations and no material time regression.

## Completion note
- `complexSVDWorkspace` now owns full and maximum singular-value evaluation for Sigma, FRD, and tuning goals.
- Tuning reads frequency-major response blocks directly and allocates only weighted matrix products when weights are present.
- Scale normalization prevents overflow and underflow in Gram formation; persistent Gonum-oracle tests cover rectangular, rank-deficient, non-symmetric, `1e-150`, `1e150`, and vector `1e200` inputs.
- Ten-sample benchstat results: MIMO weighted gain time -52.11%, bytes -30.91%, allocations -80.91%; dynamic weighted MIMO time -53.25%, bytes -14.61%, allocations -66.07%; SISO time -7.93% with unchanged allocations.

## Validation gates
- Focused frequency-SVD and tuning tests passed.
- Focused before/after tuning benchmarks compared through benchstat.
- `go fix ./...`, `go vet ./...`, and `go test -v -count=1` passed.

# Batch all-input step and impulse responses

## Goal
Make `timeResponsePlan` simulate all input channels in one state propagation pass for step and impulse responses.

## Context
Step and Impulse allocated an input history and called Simulate once per input. That repeated dispatch, intermediate allocation, and output assembly. The planner now owns discretization, delays, output layout, and the all-input simulation policy.

## Acceptance criteria
- Step and Impulse use a batched all-input kernel where applicable, with delay or exceptional paths safely routed through equivalent behavior.
- The public row ordering `j*p+i`, time grids, feedthrough behavior, continuous/discrete semantics, and delay semantics remain unchanged.
- The kernel uses stride-aware raw storage and preallocated buffers.
- Persistent parity tests cover non-symmetric MIMO systems, continuous and discrete models, gain-only systems, feedthrough, and delays.
- Focused MIMO benchmarks show fewer allocations and lower runtime; SISO has no material regression.

## Completion note
- `timeResponsePlan` now owns standard-input response policy and batches delay-free, standard multi-input systems with contiguous input-major state buffers.
- SISO, descriptor, zero-output, and delayed/internal-delay systems retain the established `Simulate` path.
- Independent-simulation parity tests cover non-symmetric continuous and discrete MIMO models, feedthrough, gain-only models, delays, Step, Impulse, and output row ordering.
- Ten-sample benchstat results: MIMO Step time -50.29%, bytes -70.51%, allocations -66.49%; MIMO Impulse time -50.27%, bytes -70.51%, allocations -66.49%. SISO Step and Impulse were about 2% faster with unchanged allocation counts.

## Validation gates
- Focused response tests passed.
- Focused before/after SISO and MIMO Step/Impulse benchmarks compared through benchstat.
- `go fix ./...`, `go vet ./...`, and `go test -v -count=1` passed.

# Make physical assembly own matrices once

## Goal
Move physical-model copy and validation ownership into `physicalAssemblyPlan` so assembly crosses one ownership boundary instead of cloning components and aggregate matrices repeatedly.

## Context
The connected path copied every component, copied into aggregate matrices, then copied the aggregate again through the public Descriptor constructor. The synchronous assembly plan can validate borrowed inputs while building an owned aggregate result directly.

## Acceptance criteria
- The plan produces an independently owned Descriptor model with no mutable aliasing to component matrices or port metadata.
- Redundant component and final aggregate clones are removed through an internal validated ownership-transfer seam.
- Constraint assembly uses stride-aware raw storage rather than repeated At/Set calls in hot loops.
- Persistent mutation tests prove that changing source components after assembly cannot change the result, and changing the result cannot change sources.
- Existing constraint, port, and validation behavior is unchanged.
- Focused physical-assembly benchmarks show fewer allocations and no material time regression.

## Completion note
- The synchronous plan validates and borrows component inputs, then creates the result at the aggregate-matrix ownership boundary.
- Internal `newDescriptorOwned` validates dimensions and descriptor shape while adopting plan-owned matrices; public `NewDescriptor` retains defensive copies.
- Augmented matrices and constraint rows now use stride-aware raw storage.
- Mutation tests cover matrices, signal metadata, and port metadata in both source-to-result and result-to-source directions.
- Ten-sample benchstat results for eight connected components: time -30.96%, bytes -38.00%, allocations -29.00%.

## Validation gates
- Focused physical-assembly tests passed.
- Focused before/after assembly benchmarks compared through benchstat.
- `go fix ./...`, `go vet ./...`, and `go test -v -count=1` passed.

# Integrate the numerical architecture and performance audit

## Goal
Close the audit with repository-wide correctness, static-analysis, and benchmark evidence, and record why other routines remain unchanged.

## Context
The codebase-wide inventory found five evidence-backed opportunities. Most remaining solver time is inside LAPACK/BLAS calls with existing reusable workspaces; changing those without a demonstrated bottleneck would increase risk without an architectural payoff.

## Production routine-family classification

### Changed after measurement or oracle failure
- Riccati and optimal-control kernel: `riccati.go` now routes singular or poorly conditioned DARE problems through an extended symplectic pencil and ordered generalized Schur decomposition while retaining the fast regular path.
- Frequency sweep: `frequency.go` now owns the state-space versus transfer-function kernel decision and reusable short-sweep workspace.
- Complex singular values and tuning: `frequency_svd.go` and `tuning_goal.go` share one scaled, reusable complex-SVD owner and flat frequency-response storage.
- Standard time responses: `response.go` owns Step/Impulse policy and batches delay-free MIMO propagation while retaining established exceptional paths.
- Physical assembly: `physical_assembly.go` and the internal seam in `state_space_utils.go` establish one validated matrix-ownership boundary.

### Existing deep owners; intentionally unchanged
- Core model, validation, domain, descriptor, metadata, and sampled layouts: `ss.go`, `descriptor.go`, `errors.go`, `names.go`, `time_domain.go`, `signal_metadata.go`, `sampled_data.go`, `sampled_response.go`, `sampled_signal.go`, `doc.go`.
- Delay representation, conversion, topology, and safe feedback: `delay.go`, `delay_bank.go`, `delay_conversion_policy.go`, `delay_topology.go`, `delay_visibility.go`, `pade.go`, `thiran.go`, `feedback_lft.go`, `safe_feedback.go`, `wellposed.go`.
- Interconnection and generalized-model workflows: `connect.go`, `interconnection_topology.go`, `lft.go`, `generalized.go`, `loopsens.go`, `sumblk.go`.
- Conversion and realization workflows: `augstate.go`, `canon.go`, `conversion_plan.go`, `convert.go`, `inv.go`, `poly.go`, `polynomial_channel.go`, `pzmap.go`, `realization_policy.go`, `transfer.go`, `transform.go`, `zpk.go`.
- Matrix equations, decompositions, balancing, reduction, and zeros: `balance.go`, `ctrbobsv.go`, `eigdecomp.go`, `gramian.go`, `lyapunov.go`, `matlog.go`, `matrix_equation_problem.go`, `minimal.go`, `modal_reduction.go`, `modsep.go`, `prescale.go`, `qr_colpivot.go`, `rq_rowpivot.go`, `sminreal.go`, `ssbal.go`, `stability.go`, `stabsep.go`, `staircase.go`, `zeros.go`. Profiles place the remaining cost in LAPACK/BLAS kernels; these routines already centralize workspace, policy, or result construction.
- Frequency and robust analysis outside the changed sweep/SVD paths: `energy_policy.go`, `frd.go`, `freqrestest.go`, `loop_analysis.go`, `margin.go`, `norms.go`, `nyquist.go`, `passivity.go`, `rlocus.go`.
- Simulation and time-response analysis outside standard-input batching: `gensig.go`, `simulate.go`, `response_info.go`; delay dispatch and general input histories remain cohesive and benchmark-stable.
- Estimation, identification, local approximation, and random models: `covar.go`, `covariance_policy.go`, `ekf.go`, `linearize.go`, `local_approx.go`, `observer.go`, `random.go`, `sysid.go`.
- Controllers and synthesis outside DARE: `controller.go`, `controller_observer_policy.go`, `h2syn.go`, `hinfsyn.go`, `lqg.go`, `pid.go`, `pidtune.go`, `smith.go`, `synthesis_partition.go`, `tunable.go`, `tuning.go`.
- Collections and matrix utilities: `model_array.go`, `matutil.go`; ModelArray inherits the Step improvement without a second implementation.

This classification accounts for all 97 production Go files.

## Accuracy evidence
- SciPy/SLICOT-style generalized-pencil DARE tests cover singular A with cross term and ill-conditioned non-symmetric A; regular cases retain the existing ordered-Schur path.
